A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BFtS research work despite the changed title and organization. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and rendered figures support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original synthetic-graph and real-dataset experiments, including fairness–accuracy comparisons, imputation accuracy, runtime measurements, and ablations.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds random-missingness comparisons and a BAIL fairness–utility experiment.

M1.justification: The three-player architecture, losses in Equations 1–7, no-sensitive-information adaptation, and alternating training procedure remain unchanged. The low-degree missingness heuristic already appeared in v3 Section 4.1; its formalization in v4 does not introduce a different algorithm.

E1.justification: The synthetic task and six real datasets are retained. v4 adds actual evaluation under missing completely at random in Figure 2 and a complete-sensitive-data reference scenario on BAIL in Figure 3; random missingness was previously discussed without this comparison.

E2.justification: v4 Figure 3 adds an evaluated fair adversarial model trained with complete sensitive information as a comparison reference. The existing benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged; newly discussed FairAC and FairSAD are not added to the reported benchmark comparisons.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs compare random and degree-based masking at matched observed fractions, and sweep beta on BAIL with 30% observed sensitive values against a complete-data control. Existing labeled-sample counts, architectures, model-selection procedures, and evaluation metrics are retained.

E4.justification: v4 adds focused analyses of whether adversarial missingness obscures bias more than random missingness and how beta controls utility costs relative to complete-data training. Existing parameter sensitivity, observed-fraction, synthetic assortativity, and kernel-PCA analyses are retained, including material moved to the appendix.

E5.justification: Table 6 gains ± uncertainty entries where v3 reported only point estimates. Both appendices retain the statement that results average 10 runs; no increase in runs or new significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v4 adds findings from Figures 2–3 and revises real-data ablation values in Table 6: GERMAN LDAM F1 changes from 0.81 to 0.74 and percentage demographic-parity gap from 1.80 to 2.74, without a documented protocol revision. BAIL BFtS equality-of-opportunity uncertainty also changes from ±0.00 to ±0.01 in v3 Table 4/v4 Table 3. Most benchmark results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v4 Section 3 introduces formal AMMCB and AMMBD optimization problems and a new NP-hardness claim. Appendix A adds a coverage-based minimum-k-union reduction and approximation discussion. The earlier BFtS minimax and Jensen–Shannon analyses are largely retained as renumbered theorems and corollary.

C1.justification: v4 makes theoretical and empirical investigation of adversarial missingness a central contribution, expanding the paper beyond proposing robust imputation. Its abstract explicitly conditions the fairness–accuracy advantage on adversarial missingness. The BFtS framework and ability to operate without sensitive information remain core claims.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly acknowledges overestimation of true bias on BAIL and explains the resulting utility trade-off controlled by beta. It adds limitations concerning large-scale evaluation and guarantees beyond demographic parity, plus a risk of inferring private information. These qualifications were absent from v3.

D1.justification: The disclosed software, hardware, dataset construction, network depth, dropout, labeled-sample counts, and hyperparameter-selection information are retained. The same anonymous repository link moves from v3's experiment section to v4's appendix Reproducibility paragraph; no changed access information is documented.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning around fairness attacks, discussing poisoning, backdoors, structural perturbations, NIFA, and FATE, and claiming novelty for attacks restricted to sensitive-value missingness. It also adds FairAC, FairSAD, missing-data fairness, and active-learning references while dropping some earlier graph-background citations.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are rewritten around adversarial missingness, with a dedicated section preceding BFtS. GNN preliminaries, metric definitions, the training algorithm, imputation accuracy, and kernel-PCA discussion move into the appendix. Method subsections and the conclusion are also reorganized.

P2.justification: v4 switches from two-column to single-column presentation, expands Figure 2 from two to four heatmaps, adds Figure 3, and redraws the architecture diagram. Figures and tables are resized and relocated, including the appendix PCA plot and imputation table. Table 1 changes to percentage and finer-precision display.

improvement.justification: The added missingness comparison, complete-data control, ablation uncertainty, and explicit limitations improve evidential clarity. However, the new central hardness argument has unresolved problems: Appendix A assigns every constructed point the positive class without explaining how coverage then controls demographic-parity bias, and its approximation implication conflicts with Section 3. These theoretical reliability concerns coexist with useful empirical and reporting improvements, preventing a confident net quality judgment.
